senses.gloss:
pṛthvī
(‘daughter of [the king] पृथु;’ ‘[that whose] quality is hardness or solidity’)
------------------------------------------
This word has generally been used in two senses: the element earth, being one of the five fundamental elements involved in च्रेअतिओन्; and the earth in which we live. For the former, see BHŪTA.
The latter is said to comprise seven dvīpas or islands known as: जम्बूद्वीप, Plakṣadvīpa, Śālmalīdvīpa, Kuśadvīpa, Krauñcadvīpa, Śākadvīpa and पुष्कर-द्वीप.
All these seven dvīpas are surrounded by different oceans like Lavaṇasamudra (ocean of salt-water).
Bhāratavarṣa (India) is in the जम्बूद्वीप.

Pṛthvīgītā
(‘Song of [Mother] Earth’)
------------------------------------------
This short work of 14 verses is a part of the Bhāgavata (vide 12.3.1-14). It is classed among the minor Gītās spread over the Mahābhārata and the Bhāgavata.
Śuka, the narrator of the Bhāgavata to the king परीक्षित्, describes in this section how भूदेवी or the मोथेर् Earth derisively speaks about the kings and emperors who ruled over her and then disappeared into the void.
The teaching may be summarised as follows:
Seeing the kings who are engaged in thinking of conquering her, भूदेवी (Mother Earth) laughs, saying, ‘Ah! These kings who are playthings in the hands of Death, want to conquer me!’
‘Eventhough these kings may be learned ones, since they are extremely attached to their flimsy bodies perishable like foam, their desires will be in vain.
‘They think—“After first practising self-control, we will then conquer the ministers of the enemy kings. Then we will conquer the commanders of the armies, and the influential subjects thereby removing all obstacles to power.
“In this way, gradually we will conquer the whole earth bordered by the seas.” With their hearts dominated by such ambitions they fail to notice Death standing nearby.
‘Some kings, even after conquering me—who has subjugated all the land up to the seas—enter into the sea to conquer the islands there. However, this is nothing compared to the conquest of oneself, for which मोक्ष or लिबेरतिओन् is the fruit.
‘The (fourteen) मनुस् and their sons left me and went the way they came from. And, the foolish people conquer me through wars!
‘The evil kings thinking (due to attachment) that the kingdom is theirs, fight even with their fathers or sons or brothers, for my sake.
‘Saying that the entire earth belongs to them, these foolish ones quarrel among themselves and even kill one another, for my sake.
‘Many Kings 1 like पृथु and Purūrava, right up to the rākṣasa kings, who were all-knowing and heroic, considering me as belonging to them, ultimately left, leaving only their names and stories behind.’

Pṛthu
------------------------------------------
The king Vena of the Sūryavaṁśa or the solar race was an atheist and an inveterate sinner. Hence the sages killed him by the power of their तपस् or austerity and created the king पृथु out of his dead body, also by using the same power.
Pṛthu was crowned as the emperor of the whole earth. He was the first king who organised a State and a government.
After he became the emperor, the people of the earth who had been famished approached him for ड़ोओद्. When he learnt that the earth had been swallowing all the seeds sown, instead of allowing them to grow (being angry with the evil people then living on earth), he was about to attack it and punish it.
The earth however, appeared before him in the form of a cow, apologised and requested him to milk her and get whatever he wanted.
Pṛthu as also the sages and others—like the ṛṣis (sages), देवस् (gods), दैत्यस् (demons), गन्धर्वस् (demigods) and others—‘milked’ her and got whatever they wanted. The ‘milk’ thus got was: agricultural crops, वेदस्, सोम juice, strength, alchoholic drinks, मुसिच्, offerings fit for śrāddha ceremonies, yogic powers and so on.
In other words, the earth (or the created world) gave all things to all persons!
From that day the earth came to be known as पृथ्वी or Pṛthivī, the daughter of the emperor पृथु.
Other achievements of पृथु were: making the uneven earth into a plane ground, च्रेअतिओन् of villages and towns with all the facilities for civilised living, protection from fears and dangers, as also the performance of many वेदिच् सच्रिड़िचेस्.
His hundredth अश्वमेध sacrifice was disrupted by इन्द्र, the king of gods in हेअवेन्. Hence he got angry and was about to destroy him (Indra) when ब्रह्मा (the four-faced creator) appeared and brought about a reconciliation between them. Lord विष्णु also appeared in his Yāgaśālā (sacrificial shed) and was worshipped by him.
After giving suitable advice to his subjects and receiving spiritual instructions from the great sage Sanatkumāra, पृथु coronated his eldest son Vijitāśva as the next king. Then he retired to the forest along with his queen Arci, performed तपस् or austerities, ultimately attaining the highest divine world.
This story of पृथु is given in detail in the Bhāgavata (4.15-23) and in the Viṣṇupurāṇa (1.13).
